title: Fatima, Before You Leave, Give Me Some Joy
intro: Al-Muthaqqib asks Fatima for a little time before she leaves and follows the women’s litters with his eyes until they disappear. He turns to his own camel, studies the marks her body makes on the ground and gives her a voice to complain about the journey. At its end he asks Amr to declare the terms of their friendship. The Mufaddaliyat commentators identify Amr with the king Amr ibn Hind, though al-Asma'i doubted that anyone would have spoken so freely to that king.

translation: Fatima, before you leave, give me some joy.
Denying me what I ask is like your going already.
1.sharh: There is still time before she leaves, but her presence is worth little to him if she withholds even a word. The short call “Fatim” lets the plea begin on intimate terms.

translation: Give me no promises that will prove false,
for summer winds to carry away before they reach me.
2.sharh: Promises seem to be on their way to him when the wind intervenes. Al-Asma'i connects summer with dusty winds from which a man waiting for rain receives nothing.

translation: If my left hand went against me
the way you do, I would never join it to my right.
3.sharh: He could scarcely choose a closer attachment than that of his own two hands. Even that bond, he insists, depends on their being able to work together.

translation: I would cut it off and tell it, “Go.”
That is how I turn from anyone who turns from me.
4.sharh: He speaks to the severed hand. The command to depart sounds like the word for Fatima’s departure in the opening, turning a separation suffered into one he could choose.

translation: Whose women’s litters rise into view from Subayb,
so long in making their way out of the valley?
5.sharh: First the litters come into view, then the long procession slowly clears the valley. The travellers’ identity matters less at this distance than the time it takes them to pass.

translation: They went by Sharaf, then Dhat Rajl,
and left al-Dharanih on their right.
6.sharh: He can no longer keep the women beside him, but still knows the turns their caravan takes. The place left on the right gives the itinerary a traveller’s point of view.

translation: So they looked as they crossed Falj,
as though their loads were riding aboard ships.
7.sharh: The breadth of the crossing lets him see the loaded animals move together. Their steady rise and fall suggests cargo riding high on ships.

translation: Ships they resemble, those Bactrian camels,
with their broad backs and broad-sutured skulls.
8.sharh: He brings us close enough to see what prompted the first impression. The camels have the breadth of hulls across both their backs and the seams of their skulls.

translation: The women sit snugly in their litters,
the death of every brave man brought low.
9.sharh: They sit as quietly as birds settled on a perch. Their stillness makes a startling counterpart to what their beauty does to a man known for courage.

translation: Like gazelles that linger behind among wild lote trees,
they reach for the branches hanging near.
10.sharh: The gazelles have fallen behind the herd and have time to browse. The small movement towards a low branch lets us see the women turn and stretch their necks.

translation: They spread one curtain and let another fall,
then pierced little peepholes for their eyes.
11.sharh: They arrange their own field of vision, screened from view but able to look out. Al-Asma'i traces the poet’s sobriquet, “the piercer”, to the verb in this line.

translation: Despite their wrongs, they are much sought after,
those women with long tresses and braids.
12.sharh: He calls their refusals an injustice from the lover’s point of view. Desire survives the rebuff, and his eye still holds the precise shapes of their long dressed hair.

translation: And gold glints on a breast
the colour of ivory, smooth and uncreased.
13.sharh: The necklace position lets two colours show in one glimpse. The gold catches the light against skin seen as smooth, pale ivory.

translation: If ever they get away with a pledge
dear to him, it will be long coming back.
14.sharh: The women carry off something like a pledge of value, understood as the lover’s heart. The language of a recoverable deposit makes its long absence more pointed.

translation: A diversion with which I feather my arrows.
They outdo the long-necked beauties of the camp.
15.sharh: The first half picks up the pursuit of the women three verses earlier. Courting them is a pastime for which he feathers his arrows. They outshine the beauties of the camp who lift their long necks like gazelles.

translation: They climbed a ridge and sank into a hollow,
scarcely stopping for a midday rest.
16.sharh: The terrain alternately reveals the women and removes them from sight. With barely a halt through the heat of noon, the procession gives him little chance to catch up.

translation: I spoke to one of them, my saddle already bound
for a noon heat I had set my forehead to face.
17.sharh: He gets one last word with an individual woman. His gear is fastened and he is already facing the heat, so the words belong to someone quite ready to leave himself.

translation: “If you cut the cord between us, perhaps
I shall still have my own self for company.”
18.sharh: She can end their bond. What he hopes to retain is command of his own person, a pointed answer to the heart carried off as a pledge.

translation: Shed the burden of care with a powerful she-camel,
huge and solid as a smith’s hammer.
19.sharh: The instruction to ride away changes the direction of the poem. The first detail of the camel is sheer solidity, made palpable in the weight of a smith’s hammer.

translation: Her quick gait never fails, as though a cat
raced beside her, clawing at the girth.
20.sharh: A little cat keeping pace beside an enormous camel gives a reason for every quickened step. Its imagined claws at the girth are stimulus enough.

translation: What clothed her in that high, matted hump
was crushed dark date-stone feed with pounded fodder.
21.sharh: Food has become something visible on the animal’s back, a hump with thick wool. The preparation of her feed explains the reserves on which the journey draws.

translation: When her gear slips I fasten a breast-strap
ahead of the breastbone, to steady the loose girth.
22.sharh: When the main girth slackens, a strap to the breast keeps it from slipping back. This is a rider attentive to what happens to the saddle over miles of travel.

translation: The marks her calloused pads leave
are like the roost of dark sandgrouse bound early for water.
23.sharh: A couching camel touches earth at several separate pads. The little hollows together could be where dark sandgrouse spent the night before flying off to drink.

translation: A deep intake of breath from her would sever
the plies of the tough, ridged leather strap.
24.sharh: A single breath expands her chest against the plaited girth. Each detail that makes the leather tough also tells us the strength he attributes to her lungs.

translation: She strikes the veins by her flanks with scattered pebbles,
their ringing has a hoarse note to it.
25.sharh: The stones her feet throw up strike her own flanks. A dull, rough note within their clatter lets the listener hear some of them landing on flesh.

translation: What her forefeet fling away looks like
stones a hired hand hurls at a stray camel.
26.sharh: The force and range of the flying stones suggest a herdsman driving a stranger’s camel from a trough. A second interpretation sees fragments flying from a mill instead.

translation: She screens with her thick tail, always switching,
the opening of a camel whose young do not thrive, dry of milk.
27.sharh: The switching brush of the tail screens the space between her thighs. He knows her history as well as her outline, including her poor luck with calves and her lack of milk.

translation: When the flies begin their song you hear
something like doves calling on their nests.
28.sharh: After the stones and the girth comes a finer sound, flies humming like nesting doves. Al-Asma'i also took the word for “fly” as the tip of a canine tooth and heard the teeth grinding.

translation: I let her have the rein and she slept,
as was her way when dawn began to show.
29.sharh: A slack rein is enough to tell her that work has stopped. The rest comes at first light, giving a glimpse of the night travelling that will account for her complaint.

translation: Where she couched looks like a bridle laid down
on the gravel and the hard, rising ground.
30.sharh: On such unyielding ground her resting shape occupies surprisingly little space. Her stretched neck and scattered pressure points suggest a bridle laid out on the stones.

translation: The saddle and its straps on her might be
on a long, oiled hull that rides the waves with ease.
31.sharh: The ship image from the departing caravan returns with the rider aboard. The saddle and straps could be gear on the long greased hull of a seaworthy vessel.

translation: Its prow splits the water and rides
the crests of every broad, swelling wave.
32.sharh: The metaphor takes over for a whole line. As the prow cuts into the water and lifts again, we feel the motion the camel’s rider has been feeling.

translation: She goes long-necked, the vein between her thigh muscles showing,
pushing on with spine and heart-vein.
33.sharh: On a well-fleshed camel the divided masses of thigh muscle make the vein between them conspicuous. The verse carries that inspection inward to the tissues on which movement and life depend.

translation: When I get up at night to saddle her,
she sighs the sigh of a grieving man.
34.sharh: A familiar movement from the rider makes her anticipate another night’s work. After so long looking at her body, he hears a sound that grants her an inner life.

translation: She says as I draw the girth round her,
“Is this forever his way of life and mine?
35.sharh: Her first words grow out of something she can feel against her body. She calls it their common way of life, although only one of them can decide when to leave.

translation: Is the whole of time just unloading and setting out?
Will he never spare me, never look after me?”
36.sharh: The camel reduces a traveller’s adventures to two endlessly repeated jobs. The question of who bears the cost is now put in the voice of the one carrying the load.

translation: My idle pursuits and her hard work have left her
like a gatekeepers’ lodge plastered in clay.
37.sharh: His amusements have meant real labour for her. The blocklike gatehouse gives some readers an image of stubborn solidity, others the bare outlines left by hard travel.

translation: I doubled back the rein and set down my saddle,
with a cushion to prop my right side.
38.sharh: The rein, the saddle and the cushion take the place of the long catalogue of her anatomy. We see how the rider arranges himself during the halt.

translation: I set off with her beside a road running straight away,
over its flat stretches and its hard ridges,
39.sharh: The way stretches out through flats and ridges as they take the road again. The destination is kept back for another beat.

translation: towards Amr, and from Amr she came to me,
quick to come to a man’s aid and sound in judgement.
40.sharh: The giver of the camel is also the man she is carrying him back to. Amr earns praise for two different capacities, acting in an emergency and deliberating soundly.

translation: Either be a true brother to me,
so I know what lean or fat I have in you,
41.sharh: He wants to know what the relationship really yields. Lean meat and fat give the experienced judge of animals a precise vocabulary for what a friend can expect.

translation: or else cast me off and take me for an enemy.
I shall watch out for you, and you for me.
42.sharh: Open enmity would at least give each man the same knowledge. The last two verbs exchange their subjects and objects, setting them face to face on equal terms.

translation: When I set my face towards something, I cannot tell,
seeking good, which of the two draws near me,
43.sharh: He widens the uncertainty between two friends into the uncertainty of undertaking anything. Naming “the two” before disclosing them keeps the listener waiting with him.

translation: whether it is the good I am seeking,
or the evil that is seeking me.
44.sharh: In the first half the speaker does the seeking. In the second he is the one being sought, a reversal that leaves even this resolute traveller uncertain of his destination.

1.1.1.head: فاطِمَة
1.1.1.meaning: Fatima, addressed by the shortened vocative Fatim.

1.1.3.head: بَين
1.1.3.meaning: Separation, specifically the departure about to take place.

1.1.4.head: مَتَّعَ
1.1.4.meaning: Gave someone a little enjoyment, here time or conversation before parting.

2.2.3-4.head: رِياحُ الصَّيف
2.2.3-4.meaning: “Summer winds”, bringing dust and carrying away what is insubstantial.

3.1.4.head: شِمال
3.1.4.meaning: The left hand, paired with the right hand below.

4.1.4.meaning: “Depart”, a command addressed to the hand as feminine.

4.2.2.head: اِجتَوى
4.2.2.meaning: Found a place or a person’s company distasteful.

5.1.2.head: ظَعينَة
5.1.2.meaning: A travelling litter or the woman travelling in it.

5.1.5.head: صُبَيب
5.1.5.meaning: Subayb, a watering place in northern Arabia. The reciter’s card gives Subayb, a pronunciation al-Tusi heard from transmitters of the poem. Shakir and Harun print Dubayb.

6.1.3.head: شَراف
6.1.3.meaning: Sharaf, a watering place on the way towards Iraq.

6.1.4-5.head: ذات رَجل
6.1.4-5.meaning: Dhat Rajl, a stopping place on the route after Sharaf.

6.2.2.head: الذَّرانِح
6.2.2.meaning: Al-Dharanih, a place the caravan leaves off to its right.

7.1.5.head: فَلج
7.1.5.meaning: Falj, a valley in eastern Arabia.

7.2.2.head: حُمول
7.2.2.meaning: Camels viewed together with their loads and litters.

8.1.4.head: بُخت
8.1.4.meaning: Bukht, large Bactrian or crossbred camels.

8.2.2.head: أَبهَر
8.2.2.meaning: A main vessel of the back, used here for its breadth.

9.1.3.head: رِجازَة
9.1.3.meaning: A woman’s camel litter or travelling seat.

9.1.4.head: واكِنَة
9.1.4.meaning: Settled on a perch, of a woman at ease in her litter.

10.1.2.head: خَذَلَ
10.1.2.meaning: Stayed behind the rest of the herd.

10.1.4.head: ضال
10.1.4.meaning: Wild lote trees, browsed by gazelles.

10.2.1.head: ناشَ
10.2.1.meaning: Reached for something close at hand.

11.1.2.head: كِلَّة
11.1.2.meaning: A fabric screen spread over a litter.

11.2.2.head: وَصوَصَة
11.2.2.meaning: A tiny peephole in a curtain or face covering.

12.1.3.head: الظِّلام
12.1.3.meaning: Unfair treatment or rebuff. The word here is distinct from darkness.

12.2.1.head: طَويلَة
12.2.1.meaning: Long, here referring to the length of their hair.

13.1.5.head: تَريب
13.1.5.meaning: The upper chest where a necklace rests.

13.2.5.head: غَضَن
13.2.5.meaning: A crease or wrinkle in the skin.

14.1.3.head: فاتَ
14.1.3.meaning: Got clear away from someone, carrying the pledge.

14.1.5.head: رَهن
14.1.5.meaning: A pledge held as security, here the lover’s heart.

15.2.2.head: مُرشِقَة
15.2.2.meaning: A gazelle craning her neck, hence a beauty with that bearing.

15.2.4.head: قَطين
15.2.4.meaning: The people staying or travelling together.

16.1.2.head: رُباوَة
16.1.2.meaning: A rise or ridge of land.

17.1.4.head: رَحل
17.1.4.meaning: A camel saddle together with its travelling gear.

18.2.3.head: مُصحِبَة
18.2.3.meaning: Compliant or keeping company, of his own self remaining at his command.

18.2.4.head: قُرون
18.2.4.meaning: One’s own self in the traditional explanation of this line.

19.2.3.head: قَين
19.2.3.meaning: A smith, here the user of the hammer.

20.1.2.head: وَجيف
20.1.2.meaning: A swift gait of a camel.

20.2.3.head: وَضين
20.2.3.meaning: The broad woven girth that holds a camel saddle on.

21.1.2.head: تامِك
21.1.2.meaning: High and full, of a well-developed hump.

21.2.2.head: رَضيح
21.2.2.meaning: Crushed date stones used as camel fodder.

21.2.4.head: لَجين
21.2.4.meaning: Leaves beaten and mixed into fodder.

22.1.5.head: سِناف
22.1.5.meaning: A breast-strap securing the saddle against slipping backwards.

23.1.3.head: ثَفِنَة
23.1.3.meaning: A calloused pad that takes weight when a camel kneels.

23.2.1.head: مُعَرَّس
23.2.1.meaning: A place where travellers or birds settle late in the night.

23.2.4.head: جون
23.2.4.meaning: Dark-coloured, of sandgrouse understood from the description.

24.2.1.head: قُوَّة
24.2.1.meaning: A ply, one of the strands making up a strap.

24.2.2.head: نِسع
24.2.2.meaning: A broad plaited leather strap for tying the saddle.

25.1.2.head: حالِب
25.1.2.meaning: A flank vein, here the two parts struck by the flying grit.

25.1.3.head: مُشفَتِرّ
25.1.3.meaning: Scattered and flying apart, applied to the pebbles her feet cast up.

26.1.2.head: نَفِيّ
26.1.2.meaning: What is sent flying, here loose stones.

26.2.2.head: غَريبَة
26.2.2.meaning: A stray camel at another herd’s trough. Another gloss makes it a borrowed mill.

27.1.3.head: خَطَران
27.1.3.meaning: A camel’s continual switching of its tail.

27.1.4.head: جَثل
27.1.4.meaning: Bushy, of the hair of the tail.

27.2.3.head: مِقلات
27.2.3.meaning: A female few of whose young survive.

27.2.4.head: دَهين
27.2.4.meaning: A she-camel with little or no milk.

29.1.2.head: زِمام
29.1.2.meaning: The rein used to lead or guide a camel.

29.2.3.head: سَدَف
29.2.3.meaning: The half-light between darkness and daylight, here first light.

30.2.4.head: وَجين
30.2.4.meaning: Rough, firm ground rising above its surroundings.

31.1.2.head: كور
31.1.2.meaning: A camel saddle complete with its fittings.

31.2.2.head: قَرواء
31.2.2.meaning: Long-backed, of the ship implied by the image.

31.2.4.head: دَهين
31.2.4.meaning: Rubbed with oil or grease, of the ship’s hull.

32.1.3.head: جُؤجُؤ
32.1.3.meaning: A projecting breast, hence a ship’s prow.

33.1.4.head: نَسا
33.1.4.meaning: A vessel along the thigh, visible between masses of muscle.

33.2.3.head: وَتين
33.2.3.meaning: A great artery connected to the heart.

35.1.3.head: دَرَأَ
35.1.3.meaning: Drew the girth into place to fasten it.

35.2.2.head: دين
35.2.2.meaning: A habitual practice or way of life.

37.2.1-2.head: دُكّانُ الدَّرابِنَة
37.2.1-2.meaning: “The gatekeepers’ lodge”, a raised structure at the entrance to a building.

38.2.1.head: نُمرُقَة
38.2.1.meaning: A small cushion used as an armrest.

39.1.4.head: مُسبَطِرّ
39.1.4.meaning: Stretching out at length, of the road.

39.2.4.head: مَتن
39.2.4.meaning: A ridge of hard, raised ground.

40.1.2.head: عَمرو
40.1.2.meaning: Amr, the camel’s giver. Some identify him with Amr ibn Hind. Al-Asma'i questioned that identification.

40.2.2.head: نَجدَة
40.2.2.meaning: Courage shown by answering another person’s call for help.

41.2.3.head: غَثّ
41.2.3.meaning: Lean, poor meat, a figure for scant benefit.

43.1.4.head: يَمَّمَ
43.1.4.meaning: Set one’s course towards an objective.

43.2.4.head: وَلِيَ
43.2.4.meaning: Drew near, here of what actually reaches him.
